abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: ProC6C is a multi-stage malaria vaccine designed to disrupt parasite transmission and prevent infection by incorporating three parasite proteins (Pfs230-Pro, Pfs48/45-6C, and CSP) in a single vaccine antigen. The Phase 1 clinical trial (PACTR202201848463189) conducted in Burkina Faso, showed ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M was safe, well tolerated, immunogenic and generated a functional antibody response to all three constituent antigens at the primary output (D70). As magnitude and durability are central to an efficacious malaria vaccine, analysis was expanded past the initial endpoint, to determine transmission-blocking antibodies (anti-Pfs230 and anti-Pfs48/45-6C) present through D180. Analysis of transmission-reducing activity (TRA) showed 7/20 samples remained biologically active at D180. To identify immune biomarkers for high levels of TRA, the Pfs48/45-6C IgG concentration (calculated relative to the transmission-blocking mAb TB31F) was compared among TRA positive and negative individuals. The magnitude of anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG had an excellent predictive accuracy (area under the receiver operating curve [ROC AUC] >0.8) with a threshold of 8.7 μg/ml for significant TRA. Additionally, there was significant correlation of TRA and anti-Pfs48/45 epitope I IgG concentration but not significant correlation for anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG, suggesting that vaccine-induced anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG is the main predictor of TRA. This finding was corroborated by the observation that complement had no effect on TRA in the standard membrane feeding assay (SMFA). Collectively, these efforts confirm the transmission-blocking attributes of ProC6C and suggest that an alternative dosing regimen be evaluated in future clinical trials to improve longevity of functional transmission-reducing antibodies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Malaria is a vector-borne disease caused by parasites of the Plasmodium genus. Of these, Plasmodium falciparum is the most common species and responsible for the largest public health burden worldwide.1 P. falciparum parasites are transmitted from one person to another by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Transition of the malaria parasites from the mosquito to the human host and from humans back into mosquitoes constitute two bottlenecks in the malaria parasite’s lifecycle. These bottlenecks are attractive targets for vaccination due to the low number of parasites, their extracellular location, and limited diversity of antigens accessible to the immune system.

The development of transmission-blocking vaccines (TBVs) against P. falciparum malaria is recognized as a key goal to achieving and sustaining malaria elimination,2 as most malaria cases are asymptomatic and therefore relatively unaffected by current malaria control interventions that aim to reduce the disease burden.

Malaria TBVs aim to elicit antibodies that are taken up by feeding mosquitos together with sexual stage parasites. Within the mosquito midgut, vaccine elicited antibodies bind to the native parasite proteins thereby inhibiting parasite multiplication and onwards transmission.3,4 The sexual-stage antigen Pfs48/45 is an attractive candidate for a TBV since it is involved in male fertility5 and since it is a target of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)6 and polyclonal antibodies7,8 with the capacity to prevent transmissio n of parasites to mosquitoes in the standard membrane feeding assay (SMFA), which assesses transmission-reducing activity (TRA) ex vivo.6,9,10 Additionally, immune epidemiological studies conducted in Africa7,11–15 and other regions16,17 have demonstrated that Pfs48/45 is recognized by naturally acquired antibodies and that high levels of anti-Pfs48/45 IgG antibodies were associated with an ability to reduce malaria transmission to mosquitoes in the SMFA.7,15 The clinical relevance of TBVs based on Pfs48/45 has been confirmed in Phase 1 studies where they elicited high levels of TRA.18,19

While TBVs may reduce malaria transmission, such vaccines do not offer the vaccinated individual any direct protection, as they do not alleviate clinical manifestations of malaria. It is therefore desirable to combine a TBV with an anti-infection vaccine-target such as the Circumsporozoite protein (CSP). Hence, ProC6C also contains immune dominant sequences of CSP in addition to those derived from Pfs48/45 and Pfs230.20 A Phase 1 clinical trial performed in Burkinabe adults evaluated ProC6C in two adjuvant combinations, Aluminum hydroxide alone (ProC6C-AlOH) and aluminum hydroxide together with the saponin based Matrix-M™ adjuvant (ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M). In this trial, we found that ProC6C vaccines were safe and immunogenic and that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicited the highest levels of vaccine-specific IgG.18 Previous analysis at two-weeks post third dose (D70), showed that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicited high levels of transmission-reducing antibodies18 as well as high levels of CSP-specific antibodies that were also found to be functional in preventing liver invasion.21 Those CSP-specific antibodies were also evaluated for longevity, and while the response decayed, the anti-CSP IgG concentration remained similar to those vaccinated with RTS,S/AS01 through D180.21

Exploratory endpoints analyzed during the Phase 1 clinical trial of ProC6C indicated a decrease in vaccine-specific antibody titer beyond D180 (four months post last dose of the 0, 1, 2-month regimen).18 However as longevity of transmission blocking (TB) antibodies is key to vaccine development, we further investigated the specificity, kinetics, and duration of transmission-reducing antibodies (Pfs48/45 and Pfs230) elicited by ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M from the Phase 1 trial in Burkinabe adults.

sec.title: Study approval
sec.p: The clinical trial protocol was approved in Burkina Faso by the Ministry of Health Ethical Committee for Biomedical Research (approval reference N°2021-02-034) and the National Regulatory authority, Comité Technique pour les Essais Cliniques, (approval reference N°2022–02041). The study was conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines. After study approval by competent authorities, the community assent process was initiated, including local community meetings to explain the trial to potentially eligible adults. Community assent was obtained from the local administrative structures, opinion leaders, family heads, and other community members after explanation and discussion of the study. All study participants provided written approved informed consent before any study procedures were performed and for the analysis conducted. The full inclusion and exclusion criteria are available.18

Additional details including the full study protocol are available under the initial safety and tolerability publication.18 Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) reporting guidelines22 were included in the prior publication18 and also reported in the analysis conducted within this manuscript. The Clinical Trial was registered in the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry (PACTR202201848463189).

sec.title: Study design and procedures
sec.p:
The study “Phase 1 Dose Escalating, Double-Blind, Randomised Comparator Controlled Trial of the Safety and Immunogenicity of Different Adjuvant Formulations of R0.6C and ProC6C transmission blocking vaccines candidates against Plasmodium falciparum in Adults in Burkina Faso (TBVax1)” was randomized, staggered, adjuvant-selection, dose-escalation phase 1 clinical trial conducted in the Sabou health district of Burkina Faso in healthy adults, aged 20–45 years. The full study design and protocol are available.18 The analysis reported here focuses on the participants (n = 20 each group) that received either 100 μg ProC6C-AlOH (Statens Serum Institut, Denmark) vaccine supplemented with 50 μg Matrix-MTM adjuvant (Novavax, Sweden) defined as group “G2D” or the placebo Hepatitis B vaccine, Euvax B (LG Chem, The Republic of Korea) defined as group “G2E” (Table 1). Vaccines were administered intramuscularly, three-times, four-weeks apart (D0, D28, D56). Sera was collected on D0, D14, D28, D42, D56, D70, D140 and D180.18 The safety and tolerability of the vaccines were previously reported.18 Prior analysis, including immunogenicity and transmission-blocking activity, focused on the D70 primary endpoint.18Table 1.

Study participants were evaluated for P. falciparum infection at screening and throughout the study by thick blood smear (two independent assessments). Participants that had Clinical or symptomatic malaria for this study were defined as the presence of asexual P. falciparum parasites at any parasitemia with at least one of the following symptoms: temperature of ≥37.5°C and/or one or more of the following symptoms: headache, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise, nausea, dizziness, or abdominal pain. Clinical or symptomatic malaria was be reported as an AE.18 Trial subjects with uncomplicated or severe malaria were treated according to national guidelines.

sec.title: Study sample availability
sec.p: The analysis conducted here utilized participants from the 100 µg ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) and the Hepatitis B (HepB, G2E) control groups. The primary endpoint samples consisted of: D70, (n = 20) were available from the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccine group (G2D), while 19 out of 20 samples were available from the control group (G2E) due to withdrawal of consent (n = 1). The durability endpoint (D140 and D180) samples consisted of n = 20, and n = 16 for G2D, and G2E respectively in this analysis due to loss of follow-up and sample availability.

sec.title: Immunogenicity evaluations of constituent Pfs48/45-6C and Pfs230-pro antigens
sec.p: Antigen-specific IgG antibody levels were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) as previously described.23 In brief, 96-well plates (Nunc Maxisorp Thermo scientific, Cat. No: 456537) were coated with 0.5 μg/mL of Pfs48/45-6C8,24 or Pf230-Pro as appropriate. Antibody concentrations are calculated through regression analysis using TB31F25 monoclonal antibody (mAb; serially diluted 0.2 μg/mL through 0.002 μg/mL) as a reference for antigens which include Pfs48/45-6C and Liberian immune pooled plasma for Pfs230-Pro. Antigen-specific antibodies were detected using horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated polyclonal Rabbit anti-human IgG (Agilent, cat. No.: P0218), diluted 1:3000 followed by 3,3', 5,5' tetramethylbenzidine dihydrochloride (TMB PLUS2) substrate (Kementec Solutions, Cat. No.: 4395A) and stopped after 20 minutes incubation at room temperature (RT) by adding 100 µl 200 mm H2SO4. Data was processed using Quant Assay for Windows (Version 0.7.1.4) and GraphPad Prism Version 8.3.0.

sec.title: Transmission-reducing activity (standard membrane feeding assay)
sec.p: The transmission-reducing activity (TRA) of samples from volunteers were evaluated using Protein G-purified IgGs at 15 mg/mL, the average physiological concentration of total IgGs in African American adults.26 The assay has been qualified,27 and conducted at National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). Briefly 16 to 18-day old gametocyte cultures of the P. falciparum NF54 line were mixed with purified IgGs from individual study volunteers and fed to Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes. The insectary was set at 27°C, 75% humidity, and 12 h of light and 12 h of darkness (with 15 minutes of dusk or dawn during the transition), and no additional blood meal was provided after the initial feed. Mosquitos were examined 8 days after feeding to determine oocyst counts (20 mosquitos per group). Experiments were conducted with and without human complement (31% v/v of non-heat inactivated human serum) as noted. The human serum was purchased from Interstate Blood Bank (Memphis, TN). Percent (%) inhibition of mean oocyst intensity (% TRA) was calculated as:100x[1−(mean number of oocysts in the test group)/(mean number of oocysts in the control groups IgGs from malaria naive US serum)]

sec.title: Competition ELISA
sec.p: Competition ELISA was also performed using mAb TB31F25 to measure Pfs48/45 epitope I-specific antibodies. Briefly, ELISA plates (Nunc Maxisorp, Thermo Scientific, Cat. No.: 456537) were coated with TB31F (1 µg/mL) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) overnight at 4°C. After blocking with PBST (PBS containing 0.01% Tween 20, Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. No.: P7949-500 mL) supplemented with 3% skim milk (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat. No.: 70166-500 G), serially diluted serum samples in PBST containing 1% skim milk and 20 ng/mL Pfs48/45-6C8 were then added to the plates for 1 hour at RT. Serial dilutions of mAb TB31F were also added under identical conditions as a standard. Following the primary incubation, a His-tagged antibody conjugated to HRP (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat. No.: 130-092-783; 1:3000 dilution) was added. The reaction was developed using TMB PLUS2 substrate (Kementec Solutions, Cat. No.: 4395A) for 20 minutes, then stopped by adding 200 mm H₂SO₄. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm. Data were analyzed using Quant Assay for Windows (Version 0.7.1.4) and GraphPad Prism (Version 8.3.0). Pfs48/45 epitope I-specific antibody concentrations were calculated through regression analysis using the TB31F28 mAb as a standard.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The limit of detection (LOD) for the Pfs48/45-6C and Pfs230-Pro ELISA were 0.04 arbitrary units (a.u.) and 0.75 a.u., respectively. Any values less than the LOD were assigned as half of the LOD values (0.02 and 0.38, respectively) for the analysis. For the comparisons of ELISA data, log-transformed ELISA titers were used for all analyses.

To compare data from two groups at the same time point, an unpaired t-test was utilized, while One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test were performed for more than two groups. Pairwise comparisons (for ELISA data) were performed using the Paired t test.

For SMFA results to determine significant TRA, the best estimate of % inhibition in oocyst density [percentage TRA], and the p values were calculated using a zeroinflated negative binomial (ZINB) random effects model described previously.29 SMFA TRA between group G2D and G2E was completed via Mann–Whitney test, and between D70 and D180 within a group or between with and without complement conditions was by Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test. The correlation between two continuous values was assessed by a Spearman rank test. p values <0.05 were considered significant.

R (Version 4.4.1, The R Foundation for Statistical Computing) was used to generate the receiver operating (ROC) curves to assess the classification of performance of the logistic regression with”pROC” R package (version 1.18.5). Optimal cutoff points were determined by Youden analysis (topleft) and with the “OptimalCutpoints” R package (Version 1.1–5). Binary values were assigned to TRA and square root values of IgG concentration utilized.

sec.title: Study participants
sec.p: The Phase 1 study of ProC6C was conducted in the Sabou health district in Burkina Faso with the full study details, primary objectives and study protocol published.18 All volunteers received three vaccinations four weeks apart. The present analysis included participants (n = 20 each group) from the 100 µg ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) and the Hepatitis B (HepB, G2E) control groups alone as prior analysis indicated G2D was the preferred formulation to move forward in clinical development. The demographics of G2D and G2E are reported in Table 1. All samples (n = 20) were available from the ProC6C vaccine group (G2D, Table 1). Due to loss to follow-up (n = 3) or withdrawal of consent (n = 1) 16 of 20 samples (Table 1) were available from the control group (G2E) at D180. Blood samples were taken at baseline (D0), two weeks after each vaccination (D14, D42, D70) and at D140 and D180 to measure durability up to four months post-last dose. Plasmodium falciparum parasite presence was monitored throughout the study and reported (D0, D70, D180) in Table 1. In previous analysis, there was no observed impact on parasite impact and immunogenicity of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M.18 All study participants were treated for malaria according to the study protocol and national guidelines.18

sec.title: Dynamics of antibody responses to ProC6C constituent antigens
sec.p:
To assess the evolution of IgG antibodies against the sexual stage antigen domains of ProC6C, specific IgG was quantitated in sera from volunteers receiving 100 µg ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) or the Hepatitis B (G2E) control vaccines. IgG responses against the Pfs48/45-6C and Pfs230-Pro domains of ProC6C were determined at D0, D14, D42, D70, D140 and D180 and calculated using reference antibodies described. All volunteers receiving ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M generated Pfs48/45-6C- and Pfs230-Pro-specific IgG responses after a single administration and these responses were boosted by subsequent vaccinations with peak antibody titers at D70 (Figure 1a,c). At baseline (D0), geometric mean titer (GMT) in the vaccine and control groups were at similar levels, with 0.2 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.1 to 0.3) and 0.3 (0.2 to 0.4) for Pfs48/45-6C, and 10.1 (6.5 to 15.6) and 7.7 (5.1 to 11.7) for Pfs230-Pro, respectively (Supplementary Table S1). At D70, antigen-specific GMT in the vaccine group increased to 12.5 (9.2 to 17.1) and 49.4 (39.9 to 61.2) for Pfs48/45-6C and Pfs230-Pro, respectively (Supplementary Table S1) and the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M group (G2D) showed significantly higher titers than the control group for both antigens (p < 0.0001 for Pfs48/45-6C and p < .0001 for Pfs230-Pro by unpaired t test). As expected, antibody titers decreased over time after D70 for both constituent antigens (Supplementary Table S1). At D180, Pfs48/45-6C GMT was 4.5 (3.1 to 6.6) and Pfs230-Pro GMT was 21.6 (15.7 to 29.8) in the vaccine group (G2D). In comparison, the GMTs in the control group (G2E) were 0.4 (0.3 to 0.5) for Pfs48/45-6C and 7.8 (4.7 to 13.1) for Pfs230-Pro. Thus, ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccinated individuals (G2D) maintained significantly higher titers than those vaccinated with HepB (G2E) four months after the third vaccination (p < .0001 for Pfs48/45-6C and p = .0014 for Pfs230-Pro). Figure 1.
Dynamics of antibody responses to ProC6C constituent antigens. Antibody levels to the ProC6C constituent antigens, Pfs48/45-6C (a & b) and Pfs230-pro (c & d), in individuals immunized with ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D, geometric mean titer, GMT-blue line) or a control vaccine (G2E, GMT-black line) at each study time point (D0, D14, D42, D70, D140, and D180). GMT is indicated in supplementary table S1.

sec.title: Functional activity of paired D70 and D180 sera
sec.p:
Having shown that serum concentration of anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG antibodies remain present four month after the last vaccination (D180), it was of interest to determine whether these IgG antibodies were functional. IgG was purified from available paired D70 and D180 sera in the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (n = 20) and Hep B control (n = 16) groups, respectively and tested at physiological antibody concentrations (15 mg/mL) in the SMFA. Each individual data point represents percentage inhibition in oocyst density (TRA). Significant (p < .05) TRA is denoted by a closed circle and non-significant TRA by an open circle (Figure 2a, and Supplementary Table S2). Eighteen of twenty samples from the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M group (G2D) had a significant (p < .05) TRA at D70 while only seven of these remained significant at D180 (Figure 2a, and Supplementary Table S2). For comparison, we also tested samples (n = 16) from the HepB group (G2E), which were available at both time points. The level of TRA in the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M group was significantly higher than that in the control group (p = .0002) at D70, while there was no significant difference in TRA between these two groups (p = .513) at D180 suggesting that vaccine-induced functional immunity decline over time. Five D70 samples and three D180 samples from HepB-vaccinated individuals (n = 16) had a significant (p < .05) TRA (Figure 2a & Supplementary Table S2). When D70 and D180 TRA levels were compared within a group, there was a significant reduction in G2D (p = .001), but not in G2E (p = .782). Figure 2.
Transmission-reducing activity of antibodies. Significant TRA denoted by a closed circles and non-significant TRA by open circles. (a) The TRA for the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) and control group (G2E) is plotted for each volunteer at D70 and D180 from purified IgG at 15 mg/mL in the SMFA (with human complement) as TRA. The median for each group is indicated by a line and p values were determined by Mann Whitney test. Paired aligned dot plots showing the (b) anti-Pfs48/45-6C and (c) anti-Pfs230-pro antibody levels at D70 and D180. Individuals were categorized into 3 subgroups based on their TRA levels: “a” significant TRA at both time points; “b” significant TRA at D70 only; and “c” insignificant TRA at both timepoints. Pairwise comparisons were performed using the paired t test (log-transformed ELISA titers were used for all analyses) (d) Pfs48/45-6C antibody levels (μg/mL) for each subgroup (“+” significant TRA and “-“ non-significant TRA). Both D70 and D180 data were combined in this analysis. GMT indicated by horizontal line. Unpaired t-tests were utilized. (e) Pfs230-pro antibody levels (a.U.) for each subgroup (“+” significant TRA and “-“ non-significant TRA). Both D70 and D180 data were combined. GMT indicated by horizontal line. Unpaired t-tests were utilized; ****p < .0001, ***p < .001, ** p < .01, *p < .05, ns p > .05.

To identify immune biomarkers associated with high levels of TRA, we plotted the concentration of anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG antibodies in paired samples from those individuals who had “a” significant TRA at D70 and D180, “b” significant TRA at D70 and non-significant TRA at D180, and “c” non-significant TRA at both timepoints (Figure 2b,c). At D70, GMT of anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG was similar for group “a” 14.9 µg/mL (CI, 8.7–25.5) and “b” 13.0 µg/mL (CI, 8.0–21.2) (Supplementary Table S3). At D180, GMT anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG concentration had decreased 3.9-fold in group “b” versus 1.3-fold in group “a” suggesting that the decline in the TRA at D180 in the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccine group (G2D) was caused by a decrease in the anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG concentration (Supplementary Table S3). Although there was a general decline in anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG levels from D70 to D180, this was not significant in group “b,” suggesting that anti-Pfs230-Pro antibodies did not play a role in vaccine related TRA (Figure 2c).

The anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG was then plotted for samples with significant (+) and non-significant (-) TRA from the G2D and G2E groups (including both D70 and D180 data), respectively (Figure 2d). The concentration of anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG in ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M immunized individuals was significantly higher (p < .0001) for samples with a significant TRA compared to those with a non-significant one, while this was not observed in G2E control group (Figure 2c). The anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG antibody titers did not differ significantly between TRA positive and negative samples (Figure 2e), supporting that anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG is the main contributor to TRA.

sec.title: Functional activity relative to antibodies to ProC6C constituent antigens
sec.p:
To further investigate the relationship between antibody titers and functional activity, TRA was plotted against the anti-Pfs48/45-6C or the anti-Pfs230-Pro IgG concentration for all samples. For ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M immunized individuals, levels of anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG were strongly correlated with TRA (p < .0001, Spearman’s coefficient r = 0.7199) (Figure 3a). In contrast, anti-Pfs230-Pro antibodies were not correlated with TRA (p = .4282, Spearman’s coefficient r = 0.1288) in these individuals (Figure 3b), confirming the role of anti-Pfs48/45-6C IgG in TRA. There was no significant correlation between TRA and the concentration of Pfs48/45-6C IgG (Figure 3c; p = .9666) or Pfs230-Pro IgG (Figure 3d; p = .3990) in HepB vaccinated individuals. Figure 3.
Correlation between transmission-reducing activity and Pfs48/45-6C and Pfs230-pro specific antibodies. G2D individuals indicated in blue and G2E individuals indicated in black circles. (a) Correlation of anti-Pfs48/45-6C antibody levels with TRA at D70 and D180 in ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccinated individuals (G2D). (b) Correlation of Pfs230-pro antibody levels with TRA at D70 and D180 in ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccinated individuals (G2D). (c) Correlation of anti-Pfs48/45-6C antibody levels with TRA at D70 and D180 in control vaccinated individuals (G2E). (d) Correlation of Pfs230-pro antibody levels with TRA at D70 and D180 in control vaccinated individuals. The TRA is plotted in log of mean oocyst ratio (LMR) between control and test IgGs (y axis) respective to square root (sqrt) of antibody levels of Pfs48/45-6C or Pfs230-pro (x axis). For ease of comprehension, the y axis shows corresponding percent TRA values instead of LMR. Correlations were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation. The p value and correlation coefficient (r) in each panel are shown.

sec.title: Functional activity in relation to specific antibody measurement
sec.p:
We focused the analysis against antibody measurements (biomarkers) against Pfs48/45-6C and specifically those against epitope I as this is a major target of TB antibodies including mAb TB31F.30 Specific antibodies against epitope I were determined by a competition ELISA where serial dilutions of serum samples from individuals receiving ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) were incubated with recombinant Pfs48/45-6C and subsequently added to plates coated with TB31F. Antibody concentration was expressed as mAb equivalence units (µg/ml) calculated relative to the Pfs48/45-6C specific mAb TB31F. The level of epitope I-specific antibodies correlated (p < .0001, Spearman’s coefficient r = 0.7557) with the Pfs48/45-6C IgG concentrations (Figure 4). However, some samples showed a high signal in the Pfs48/45-6C ELISA and a low signal in the epitope I competition ELISA suggesting that the Pfs48/45-6C domain contain multiple epitopes for human antibodies. Figure 4.
Correlation between antibodies against epitope I (competition) and total Pfs48/45-6C IgG and TRA. Using the TB31F competition ELISA, D70 and D180 epitope I antibody reactivity was determined in volunteers vaccinated with ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D). The square root (sqrt) of D70 antibody levels of Pfs48/45-6C (y axis) is plotted against the sqrt of epitope I antibody levels (x axis). Antibody levels are given as TB31F equivalence (μg/mL) for Pfs48/45-6C IgG. The coefficient of correlation and p value using Spearman’s rank test are provided. The red dotted line shows a y=x.

To investigate the ability of anti-Pfs48/45 antibodies to discriminate between samples with and without significant TRA, empirical ROC curves were constructed using both anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-epitope I IgG. When all D70 and D180 samples from individuals immunized with ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M were included in the analysis, we found ROC area under the curve (AUCs) of 0.8933 (CI, 0.7954–0.9913; p < .0001) and 0.8267 (CI, 0.6996–0.9536; p < .0001), respectively. Considering a ROC AUC of greater than 0.8 as excellent,28 both antibody measures had excellent predictive accuracies (Figure 5a,b). The estimated threshold for significant TRA was 8.7 and 5.5 µg/ml for the anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-epitope I measurements, respectively using Youden’s topleft analysis. The performance characteristic of the threshold for anti-Pfs48.45-6C included a sensitivity of 0.933 (CI, 0.681–0.998) and specificity of 0.720 (CI, 0.506–0.879) while the anti-epitope I included a sensitivity of 0.867 (CI, 0.595–0.983) and specificity of 0.680 (CI, 0.465–0.851). A similar ROC curve analysis was conducted for anti-Pfs230-Pro (Supplementary Figure S1), however was found to be not significant (AUC of 0.628, p = .222). Figure 5.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Receiver operating characteristic curves were generated for the square root of IgG: anti-Pfs48/45-6C (a) and anti-epitope I (b) relative to significant TRA. (a) Anti-Pfs48/45-6C demonstrated an AUC of 0.8933 and a threshold of 8.7 μg/mL. (b) Anti-epitope I demonstrated an AUC of 0.8267 a threshold of 5.5 μg/mL. In contrast Pfs230-pro IgG did not demonstrate a high level of specificity and sensitivity (supplementary figure S1). Youden’s topleft analysis was utilized to determine the optimal threshold on the ROC curve as indicated by dot and light dotted lines. Black dotted line y=x.

Collectively, these results demonstrated that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicit IgG antibodies against the major epitope I for TB antibodies in Pfs48/45 together with antibody specificities against other Pfs48/45 epitopes.

sec.title: Effects of complement on the functional activity of sera from ProC6C vaccinated individuals
sec.p:
To distinguish between the contribution of anti-Pfs48/45 and anti-Pfs230 antibodies in TRA, samples were tested with (+C) and without (−C) complement as Pfs230 activity (but not Pfs48/45) is complement dependent.31,32 Analysis at D70 (peak response), showed there was no significant (p = .5875) difference between the levels of TRA irrespective of complement, supporting that anti-Pfs230 antibodies are of lesser importance for TRA in the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccine group (Figure 6). Figure 6.
Transmission-reducing activity of ProC6C IgG is independent of complement. The TRA of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M (G2D) sera is plotted for each volunteer at D70 with (+C) and without (−C) human complement. p values determined by Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; ns, p > .05.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: A first-in-human clinical trial demonstrated that an adult population vaccinated with ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicited high levels of transmission blocking antibodies measured in the SMFA at D70.18 However, there was no information on the longevity of these functional antibodies in the initial analysis.

Here we report on the TRA elicited by ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M through pairwise analysis of functional antibodies at Days 70 (2-weeks post-third vaccination) and 180 (4-months post-third vaccination). We found that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M delivered through three doses, each four weeks apart, resulted in peak antibodies at D70, with functional TB antibodies waning over time. At D70, 18/20 individuals had significant TRA in the SMFA, while only 7 of these maintained significant TRA at D180. Longevity of antibody titers is key to an effective malaria vaccine, and these results indicate the ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M vaccine regimen should be altered from the current regimen in future trials to evaluate the potential to improve antibody durability. Future clinical development of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M could therefore consider an altered primary immunization regimen (e.g. 0,1,6 months) to extend antibody longevity33 or an additional booster dose such as established for the hepatitis B vaccine.34

In attempt to quantitate antibodies against epitope I in the Pfs48/45-6C domain we used a competition assay with mAb TB31F. Using ROC analysis, we found that levels of anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-epitope I antibodies were excellent predictors of significant TRA with thresholds of 8.7 and 5.5 µg/ml, respectively. As expected, these thresholds for a polyclonal antibody response are higher than the 2.1 μg/mL (95%CI 1.9–2.3) concentration of the mAb TB31F which was required for 80% TRA in the recent phase I study of TB31F.25 Identifying an immune biomarker which predicts functional activity (TRA) would allow simple, high-volume comparisons between immunization regimens and vaccine doses. Overall, the predictive analysis supports previous clinical results with TB31F and suggests that the immune biomarkers identified here may be useful in future ProC6C vaccine development either individually or in combination.

As expected, we found that levels of anti-Pfs48/45-6C and anti-epitope I IgG were highly correlated. However, there were some samples with relatively high levels of Pfs48/45-6C IgG and low levels of epitope I IgG suggesting that ProC6C elicited antibodies against other Epitopes in the Pfs48/45-6C region. The finding that human anti-Pfs48/45-6C antibodies might be targeting multiple epitopes is in line with resent data published on a series of human mAbs against Pfs48/45.35 Using X-ray crystallography and competition assays with TB31F these authors identified at least two distinct epitope regions within the Pfs48/45-6C domain, one of which is different from epitope I. Whether this epitope domain is recognized by antibodies generated by ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M remains to be investigated. Similar, antibody avidity may play a role in competition of Pfs48/45-6C antibodies including to epitope I and TB31F and therefore antibody avidity should be evaluated in future studies.

In addition to the Pfs48/45-6C domain, ProC6C also contains the Pfs230-Pro domain in the N-terminal end of the fusion protein. Pfs230 is a large protein containing multiple cysteine-rich domains and an unstructured domain (Pro) in the N-terminal region.36 The detailed investigation of Pfs230 domains for functional antibodies demonstrated that the N-terminal Pro domain was sufficient to elicit complement-dependent TB activity in the SMFA.37,38 The results presented here demonstrated that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicited high levels of antibodies against the Pfs230-Pro domain. Although the Pfs230-Pro titers were high, there was no effect of complement suggesting that anti-Pfs48/45 antibodies are the main contributor to the functional activity in this ex vivo assay.

Antibodies against the sexual stages of the parasite aims to block the male/female fertilization in the mosquito midgut, or the development of the ookinete thereby preventing transmission from one person to another. While, such antibodies do not offer the vaccinated individual personal protection, reducing malaria transmission is considered a priority because the majority of malaria cases in endemic areas are asymptomatic and therefore relatively unaffected by malaria control interventions that aim to reduce the disease burden. Whereas the anti-infection vaccines (AIV), RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M provide personal protection, a multi-stage vaccine such as ProC6C which combine anti-infection and TB activities may transform the impact of vaccination from protection of vulnerable groups to a reduction of disease burden in the population by reducing the incidence of P. falciparum infection in both human and mosquito populations. The present analysis reported here, excluded the anti-infection (CSP based antibody responses) as they were previously reported for ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M21 including D70 and D180 anti-CSP IgG.

Current and planned vaccination campaigns with RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M are targeting children below 5 years of age.39,40 Considering the importance of asymptomatic school-aged children (5–15 years) in malaria transmission,41,42 the inclusion of a TBV in a multi-stage vaccine could form a rationale for including older children in future malaria vaccination studies. The TBV component(s) of a multi-stage vaccine is further important as they may block selection for AIV escape mutants as well reduce the spread of resistant parasites which may compromise effective treatment of clinical malaria in endemic countries.43

In summary we have shown that ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M elicits TRA and TB antibodies which wane over time through four-months post last dose. Thus, a new vaccination schedule using a delayed fractional dose should be considered in future trials of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M to induce high levels of functional antibodies lasting through six-month post-vaccination, especially during age-de-escalation.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: The ProC6C multi-stage malaria vaccine immunogen is a complex recombinant protein encompassing three malaria related proteins (Pfs230, CSP, and Pfs48/45). The complexity of three antigens and two vaccine objectives (transmission-blocking and anti-infection) result in a complicated dataset to analyze. Due to the rapid clinical development (two Phase 1 clinical trials in two endemic populations) and a current enrolled Phase 2 trial, a complex dataset has been generated. The authors have undertaken the approach of first demonstrating safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity to the vaccine immunogen (ProC6C). Subsequent analysis has resulted in the authors reporting the anti-infection and transmission-blocking properties separately along with durability of the antibodies generated. Future analysis should evaluate transmission-blocking and anti-infection properties to determine any correlation of the two vaccine-induced approaches. Additionally, as ProC6C has been explored in two populations (Burkina Faso and Mali), the impact of the endemic population, seasonality of malaria, and preexisting immunity should be further explored especially to evaluate any confounding factors (and prognostic) factors. Additionally, the current study was powered for safety, tolerability and immunogenicity and future studies should assess the impact of confounding and prognostic factors to assure appropriate sample size.

Due to the multi-stage malaria disruption nature of ProC6C, the vaccine is designed to be administered to both young, school-age children, and village populations (adults). Future trials will have to carefully evaluate the impact of age on vaccine-induced antibody magnitude and durability and explore the interrelationship of transmission-blocking (community) on direct personal protection.

The functional activity (TRA) as measured in the SMFA is both a labor intensive and variable assay, however it is a standardized assessment of transmission-reducing activity of malaria candidates. The physiological concentration tested here (15 mg/mL) is the average IgG concentration of Africa American Adults,26 but this concentration may be 2–3 fold higher than that observed in developed countries.44 Therefore the TRA observed at 15 mg/mL IgG may not be inferred or applicable to the exact IgG concentration required for differing populations, including younger or school-age children. Nevertheless, the SMFA allows a standardized ex vivo assessment of TBVs.

A strength of ProC6C is that it confers transmission-blocking activity and anti-infection activity in a single vaccine; while other TBVs are being explored to be administered in conjunction with RTS,S/AS01 or R21/Matrix-M. In addition, ProC6C targets novel TBV proteins (Pfs48/45) and novel CSP epitopes (major and minor repeats). Therefore, ProC6C has the ability to stand alone as a single-multi-stage vaccine or may even be explored to improve and focus CSP immune responses of other current CSP-based vaccines such as RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Comprehensive analysis of the Phase 1 trial of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M has previously shown that the multi-stage malaria vaccine is as follows: 1) safe and immunogenic,18 2) Elicits transmission blocking activity at D70,18 and elicits liver invasion inhibition through CSP-based antibodies.21 Exploratory endpoints analyzed here, indicated a decrease in TB antibody titer (Pfs48/45 and Pfs230) beyond day 140 (3 months post last dose of the 0, 1, 2 month regimen). Additionally, a small Phase 2 Controlled Human Malaria Infection (CHMI) study is currently ongoing (PACTR202404598604620) to also determine the vaccine efficacy (CSP-based antibodies) at approximately 3-months post last dose of the 0, 1, 2 month regimen. These early phase clinical results taken together, will support during age-escalation, in the pediatric population, whether altered immunization regimens to extend antibody longevity should be explored. Altering the prior trial design (0,1,2 month vaccine regimen) to a delayed third vaccination (0,1,6 months) has proven highlight successfully for the P. falciparum RH5 vaccine candidate.45,46 Further, RH5 induced a 10-fold higher vaccine specific response in infants (6–11 months) compared to UK adults.47

Further, the initial ROC analysis of anti-Pfs48/45 markers (Pfs48/45-6C and epitope I) indicate circulating biomarkers of transmission-reducing activity following vaccination with ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M can be identified. These curves and thresholds should be updated as additional trials are conducted, with the objective of finding surrogate circulation biomarkers to replace the labor intensive and variable ex vivo SMFA. Similarly, following further clinical studies of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M for anti-infection (anti-CSP based antibody responses), surrogate biomarkers representative of the anti-CSP response may be correlated to clinical outcomes, adding value to additional biomarkers following vaccination of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M which may serve to measure and monitor the vaccines functionality and also antibody longevity.
Taken together, these results suggest that age-de-escalation and a delayed third dose of ProC6C-AlOH/Matrix-M can significantly increase the magnitude and durability of specific antibodies.

bio.p: Mohammad Naghizadeh (PhD) is a Postdoc at Department of Immunology and Microbiology, University of Copenhagen with a joint appointment at the Department of Congenital diseases (SSI). From Iran, with focus on malaria protein expression, vaccine design and development, assay standardization & validation and immune responses.

Kazutoyo Miura (MD, PhD) has served as Scientific Director of the Growth Inhibition Assay and Standard Membrane Feeding Assay reference center (GIA/SMFA reference center) at the Laboratory of Malaria and Vector Research/NIAID/NIH since 2010. The GIA/SMFA reference center has been supporting blood-stage and transmission-blocking vaccine development against P. falciparum malaria by evaluating biological activity of >2,000 samples every year, from novel antigen discovery in animals to human phase 1/2 clinical trials. His expertise is malaria vaccine development, assay standardization & validation, immune responses, and statistical analysis

Ebenezer Addo Ofori is a PhD student at Department of Immunology and Microbiology, University of Copenhagen with a joint appointment at the Department of Congenital diseases (SSI). From Ghana, his focus on malaria epidemiology, serology and genetic markers.

Carole Long (PhD) is Chief, Malaria Immunology Section; Director, PATH Malaria Vaccine Initiative Standard Membrane Feeding Assay-Reference Center and Director, USAID Growth Inhibition Assay–Reference Center. Dr. Long received her Ph.D. in microbiology and immunology from the University of Pennsylvania and also did postdoctoral training there. Before joining NIAID in 1999, Dr. Long was a professor of microbiology and immunology at Hahnemann University School of Medicine (now Drexel University) in Philadelphia. She has served as president of the American Society for Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and chair of the Tropical Medicine and Parasitology Study Section. Her lab’s work focuses on immune responses to malaria parasites, particularly in those living in malaria-endemic areas, and also on identification and evaluation of possible candidate antigens for malaria vaccines.

Issaka Sagara (MD, PhD) is a professor at USTTB, University of Bamako and Researcher at the Malaria Research and Training Center, Mali. USTTB includes faculties of Medicine, Pharmacy and Basic Sciences, an Institute of Applied Science, and the research laboratories founded by the NIH/NIAID which focus on malaria, tuberculosis and retrovirology. USTTB has completed dozens of Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials and specifically three PfTBV vaccine trials involving 3 different sites in Mali as a partnership with NIAID. Issaka Sagara serves as study sponsor for malaria vaccine development projects.

Alfred B. Tiono (MD, PhD) is a Clinician and Senior Scientist at The Groupe de Recherche Action en Santé (GRAS). He has been working in the malaria field for over 10 years and has been a frequent contributor to the National Malaria control Program implementation. His current research interest involves clinical trials of malaria vaccines candidates and antimalarial drugs, development of innovative Community based interventions against malaria. The Groupe de Recherche Action en Santé (GRAS) is a private institute based in Burkina Faso, operating since 2008 in the field of health research. The scientific staff of GRAS is multi-disciplinary with well proven skills in clinical trials. They carried out, during last decade, more than 25 clinical trials for various infectious diseases (Malaria vaccines, Pneumococcal vaccines, Ebola vaccines, Typhoid fever vaccine, etc.). GRAS is currently a member of several consortia working to develop new treatments or vaccines against these diseases.

Jordan Plieskatt is contracted by the Department of Immunology and Microbiology, University of Copenhagen to aid in the development of ProC6C. He has worked in recombinant vaccine production for over two decades, predominantly targeting the neglected tropical diseases. With a focus on protein expression, purification, analytics and formulation, he has led the translation of more than a dozen vaccine candidates from R&D to clinical trails. He has conducted cGMP campaigns in the US, EU and Brazil and often provides onsite support to technology transfer and manufacturing efforts. After working more than a decade with The George Washington University, while in pursuit of vaccines against human hookworm, schistosomiasis and malaria, he built upon his familiarity with academia, government research institutes, NGOs and PDPs and formed Praestans Biosciences LLC. Today, he continues his vaccine development work in the malaria field.

Michael Theisen (PhD) is a senior researcher at the Department of Congenital diseases (SSI), with a joint appointment as a professor at Department of Immunology and Microbiology, University of Copenhagen. He has more than 30 years of experience in translating scientific discoveries into clinically tested agents, including 20+ years of biopharmaceutical discovery, lead optimization, and product development experience in malaria vaccine research and development. Beyond scientific discovery and research, he has been responsible for advancing three programs into clinical trials (including Phase 2 trials) in Europe and Africa, along with establishing consortiums and funding partnerships.
